newsitem.title: USA: British nanny pleads not guilty to murder.
newsitem.headline: British nanny pleads not guilty to murder.

text.p: A 19-year-old British nanny pleaded not guilty on Friday to a first-degree murder charge in the death of a nine-month-old boy in her care.

Louise Woodward, of Chester, England, wearing a white blouse and black slacks, her dark hair draped over her shoulders, appeared composed when she stood in a Cambridge, Massachusetts court and said "not guilty."
She is alleged to have killed Matthew Eappen last month by severely shaking him and striking his head on a hard surface, causing a skull fracture.

If convicted of first-degree murder, she would face a mandatory sentence of life in prison with no eligibility for parole. Woodward has been held without bail at a Massachusetts prison in Framingham, outside Boston.
Middlesex Superior Court Judge Hiller Zobel ordered a trial date of July 14.

Defence lawyer Andrew Good, when asked by reporters about Woodward's condition, said: "It's enormously difficult to deal with this, and enormously difficult for her to cope with this case. She's holding up well for a 19-year old girl in a foreign country."
Good told the court he would not try to have Woodward released on bail at the present time.

He also said he would submit a motion to have a grand jury indictment of first-degree murder dismissed on the grounds that the prosecution exaggerated the injuries to Eappen and did not adequately explain the difference between the murder charges.
A Middlesex County grand jury on Wednesday indicted Woodward with first-degree murder rather than the lesser charges of second-degree murder or manslaughter.
Prosecutors must now prove that she deliberately murdered Eappen or committed the act with extreme atrocity and cruelty.

"This charge is founded on a one-sided presentation to the grand jury," Good said. "In the Commonwealth statement, they claim a severity of injury, consistent with a child being dropped out of a second storey window."
But autopsy reports said Eappen had no external head injuries, he said.
Assistant Middlesex District Attorney said last month that Woodward admitted to police that she handled the baby roughly and shook him because he was fussy and she was frustrated.

Woodward called rescue workers to her employer's home in the upscale Boston suburb of Newton on Feb. 5 and told them the boy had suddenly stopped breathing after being sick all day. He was taken to hospital and diagnosed with head trauma consistent with shaken-baby syndrome.
He was on life support for four days before he died of a brain haemorrhage on Feb. 9. Autopsy reports ruled the cause of death was a blunt blow to the head.
Woodward had lived with and cared for Matthew Eappen and his two-year old brother since November.

The baby's parents, Drs. Sunil and Deborah Eappen, who both work at Children's Hospital in Boston, sat in court on Friday but did not comment to reporters. On Wednesday they urged the judge in a statement not to grant bail to Woodward saying "with no ties to the community and a consequence of a guilty verdict, we think the risk of flight is great."
